cards.title: Budget Allocation Across Ad Channels (50/20/10/20 Model)
cards.summary: Ridge's actual paid-media mix splits spend 50% Meta, 20% Google/YouTube, 10% influencer and 20% tertiary channels, each fed only up to its 'perfect level of spend.'
cards.use_when: Deciding how to split a paid acquisition budget across channels for a DTC store, or auditing whether spend is concentrated in one platform.
steps: Set a baseline mix: roughly 50% Meta, 20% Google/YouTube (search ~5% and YouTube ~15% within that), 10% influencer/podcast, and 20% spread across tertiary channels (Snapchat, TikTok, Reddit, X, Pinterest, AppLovin, linear TV). This is Ridge's mix at nine-figure scale, not a universal law.
Keep tertiary channels small and run them at roughly $1,000–$10,000/day combined, letting them ebb and flow rather than giving each a dedicated buyer.

Apply the 'next best dollar' principle: keep spending on a channel until the next incremental dollar is better spent elsewhere, then find that new channel's perfect level of spend. Revisit continuously because the right mix shifts.
Note the mix is directional: Meta spend ranged from 50% to 75% across years, and Ridge expected partner ads possibly rising toward half of spend in Q4.
For pre-scale brands, the source's own advice is to skip paid entirely and build organic short-form skill first (claimed enough to reach ~$10M/year); treat that as a strong opinion, not a rule.
Verify current platform ad products and interfaces before setting up campaigns; formats and placements change.
caveats: These percentages describe one large brand's mix and depend on margins and category; they are not benchmarks for every store.
The claim that organic alone can reach $10M/year is Ridge's founder's opinion.

cards.title: Cut Branded Search and Treat Google Shopping as Low-Incrementality
cards.summary: Ridge's incrementality holdouts found branded search is largely non-incremental and should be kept under ~1% of marketing spend, with Shopping also weak incrementally.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a paid search budget to free cash for creative or new channels, especially for a store with strong brand recognition.
steps: Separate paid search into branded and non-branded campaigns before judging performance.
Run an incrementality holdout on branded search: pause spend in a held-out geography or audience and measure whether total revenue moves.
If the holdout shows little revenue change, cut branded search to under ~1% of total marketing spend (Ridge's stated target) rather than optimizing its reported ROAS.
Treat Google Shopping skeptically when a store has strong brand awareness — many converters may be arriving anyway; test non-branded search selectively.
Consider that for a brand bigger than its category (e.g., more people search the brand than the generic term), winning generic category searches is harder and less incremental.
Repeat holdout testing periodically since incrementality shifts with awareness and competition.
Verify current Google Ads campaign structures and measurement options, as Google's tools change.
caveats: These findings come from Ridge's holdouts and may not transfer to brands with low awareness or little branded search volume.
Reported platform ROAS on branded search can look strong while contributing little incremental revenue.

cards.title: Incrementality Holdout Testing to Validate Channel Spend
cards.summary: Geo-based holdout cells (e.g., one state withheld from a channel) reveal whether spend drives incremental revenue, useful once multiple channels are in play.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep, cut or expand spend on a channel such as Meta or a tertiary network, or diagnosing whether platform-reported conversions are real.
steps: Build test 'cells': withhold a channel's spend from a matched set of geographies (e.g., North Carolina exposed vs South Carolina held out) while keeping other marketing consistent.
Compare total business revenue between exposed and held-out cells to estimate incremental revenue the channel actually caused.
Use the result to answer whether to spend the next dollar on that channel versus elsewhere — the core 'next best dollar' decision.

Consider starting once you spend across multiple channels; the source suggests the need arises when you diversify (he cites figures around $15M–$50M as when brands typically adopt it, framed as an estimate, not a fixed threshold).
Note that Meta reportedly offers free incrementality tests because it is confident in its own results; use these but understand the source of the test.
Vendors in this space (e.g., Northbeam, Measured, Haus-style holdout tools) change offerings — verify current capabilities before committing.
caveats: Results depend on matched geographies and clean experimental design; simpler state-vs-state comparisons are a simplification of more rigorous methods.
Incrementality tooling costs money; small stores may lack the volume for reliable signal.

cards.title: Spend ~1% of Budget on Measurement and Media Tools
cards.summary: Ridge's guideline is to allocate about 1% of the marketing budget to attribution, media-mix modeling and incrementality tools, on the logic that a 5% improvement pays for them.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to invest in attribution, MMM or incrementality tooling versus putting all budget into media.
steps: Carve about 1% of total marketing budget for measurement tools (multi-touch attribution, media-mix modeling, incrementality/holdout testing).
Evaluate tool spend against a simple test: if the tools improve media effectiveness by roughly 5%, they pay for themselves.

Use MMM (mixed media modeling) tools to survey all channel spend and suggest reallocation (e.g., toward TV or Snapchat); it is an older but still-used approach and, per the source, is somewhat falling out of favor relative to incrementality.
Use multi-touch attribution with clean naming conventions so spend can be compared apples-to-apples across channels and creative units.

Right-size by stage: if a store is only running Meta profitably at scale, the source suggests skip expensive measurement and put the money into creative instead; adopt incrementality tooling once spend spans multiple channels.
Verify current vendor pricing and methodology, as these platforms evolve.
caveats: The 1% figure and the 5% payback are rules of thumb from one operator, not a calculation.
MMM and incrementality methods and vendor prominence change over time; do not treat any single tool as definitive.

cards.title: Naming Convention and Creative Tagging System for Attribution
cards.summary: Tag every ad with concept, hook, thumb-stop and edit variables so attribution tools can compare creative units across platforms and find what to scale.
cards.use_when: Setting up or cleaning up ad naming conventions so paid creative tests produce comparable, actionable data across platforms.
steps: Define naming fields that describe an ad's actual units: concept/angle, hook, thumb-stop (opening image or frame), and edit variation, plus format (static vs video) if useful.
Keep other variables constant when testing a variable — e.g., run 10 different hooks with the same body and CTAs to isolate hook performance.
Structure tests as head-to-head comparisons (A/B/C...) of hooks so results can be read directly.
Load these tags into an MTA tool (Ridge uses Northbeam) so you can see, for example, that one thumb-stop performs better across all platforms and should be scaled.
Interpret the results in context: watch-time/time-to-third-second can indicate a strong thumb-stop, but if viewers watch too far (reaching the end card) it can signal the mid-video CTA is weak.
Use free ad libraries (e.g., Facebook Ads Library) and tools like Foreplay or Motion for competitive creative research; verify current interfaces before adopting.
Keep on-site CTA placement decisions separate: multiple CTAs within a video can raise on-site conversion even when view-through patterns look 'off.'
caveats: Richer tagging requires tooling and team discipline; small teams may start with simpler 3-field conventions (e.g., format, theme, hook).
Creative-analysis metrics are indicative, not definitive attribution.

cards.title: Find the 'Next Best Dollar' Across All Channels
cards.summary: Rather than maximizing one channel, pursue the perfect level of spend on every channel by comparing where each marginal dollar earns the most.
cards.use_when: Allocating incremental budget across channels or deciding whether to open a new channel (e.g., linear TV, TikTok) for a scaling store.
steps: Treat every channel as having an optimal spend level; the job is to reach it, not to max out any one platform.
Before adding budget to the current channel, ask whether the next dollar is better spent elsewhere; if yes, move it.
Fund smaller 'tertiary' channels (Snapchat, TikTok, Reddit, X, Pinterest, AppLovin, linear TV) at modest levels — around $1,000–$10,000/day combined — and let them fluctuate with performance.
Recognize platform dependency risk: when one platform was 95% of a media budget, one algorithm shift could stall the business. Diversify deliberately.
Re-run the comparison regularly because channel efficiency and creative performance keep changing.
Use incrementality results rather than platform-reported metrics to judge whether a channel deserves the next dollar.
Confirm current channel ad products and buying interfaces before expanding, as these change frequently.
caveats: Optimal channel mixes are business-specific and shift over time; there is no fixed formula.
Diversifying poorly (weak ad products, fraud-prone display, PMAX-type blended buys) can waste money — the source warns PMAX especially can mask wasteful spend.

cards.title: Build an Organic-to-Paid Creative Flywheel
cards.summary: Use organic short-form as the proving ground: post broadly, then push proven organic winners into paid (including partner/ASC campaigns).
cards.use_when: Sourcing ad creative for a new or scaling store, or deciding which creative to put paid spend behind.
steps: Publish lots of short-form organic content across platforms (Reels, Shorts, TikTok, Snapchat, Pinterest) before spending on ads.
Watch for organic winners — the source reports that 70% of its best paid ads are organic best-performers, and this is a specific brand's result, not a guarantee.
Take top-performing organic posts and run them as paid (e.g., Advantage+ / ASC campaigns) on a recurring weekly cadence to build a flywheel.
Create multiple owned or partner social accounts as creative testing ground; account follower count is reportedly irrelevant to ad performance.
Consider partner ads (running creative from two handles together) — the source expects Meta's algorithm to favor them and aimed for up to half of spend on partner ads in a peak period.
For high-AOV stores with too little purchase signal to test at scale, seed concepts organically and/or optimize to add-to-cart or page-view conversions to get more signal.
Verify current Meta/partner-ad setup steps, as the product changes.
caveats: The '70% of best ads are organic winners' figure is Ridge-specific.
The claim organic content alone can carry a brand to ~$10M is the founder's opinion and not a benchmark.

cards.title: Feed Meta Volume and True Creative Contrast
cards.summary: Meta rewards radically different creative at high volume; incremental tweaks (color, angle) register as the 'same' ad to the algorithm.
cards.use_when: Scaling paid creative production and deciding how many and how different ads to launch.
steps: Produce at high volume: Ridge launches hundreds of ads weekly to find the occasional top performer; the source says a top ad may cap around $100k, so consistent winners require constant new creative.

Prioritize true contrast: test ads with entirely different concepts, casts (e.g., 'just guys' vs 'just girls'), selling points and pain points — the algorithm reportedly treats minor variations (background color, slight angle) as the same ad.
Invest most in the opening: thumb-stop and hook matter most because they reach new people; middle and end matter less.
Test hooks head-to-head with body and CTAs held constant to isolate what works.
Run multiple production sources simultaneously (in-house studio, agencies, UGC creators) rather than relying on one.
For early-stage brands, make your own ads first — the source argues consumer brands are 'marketing companies' that shouldn't outsource core creative and paid media.
Confirm current Meta ad-system behavior and creative best practices, since the algorithm changes.
caveats: High-volume creative production requires budget and team; smaller stores must adapt the principle to their capacity.
Claims about how the algorithm classifies creative are the operator's interpretation and subject to change.

cards.title: Product Launch Criteria: CAC vs LTV Classification and Product-Mix Focus
cards.summary: Classify products as acquisition (CAC) versus retention/LTV drivers, and track revenue share from new categories to shift from a single-product brand to a multi-line business.
cards.use_when: Deciding which products to launch, how to classify them, and which metrics to watch for product-mix evolution.
steps: Classify each product by role: a 'CAC product' acquires new customers (high AOV, low repeat) while an 'LTV product' drives repeat purchase and category expansion with broader appeal.
Track the share of revenue coming from new product categories (not just the flagship) to gauge whether the brand is evolving beyond a single hero product.
Observe the Yeti pattern: coolers were the entry hero but water bottles became ~70% of revenue — using one product to acquire and others to expand.
Watch new-customer acquisition by product and by market (e.g., 'how many of the newest product did I acquire today, in each country') as a core metric.
When repeat purchase is structurally limited (one-and-done products like wallets), add adjacent products to create repurchase paths rather than pushing the same item repeatedly.
Set a target like returning-customer revenue share (the source aims for 50%) and treat it as a gold-standard metric for category expansion.
Confirm which metrics your own analytics and attribution tools surface before committing.
caveats: This framework comes from Ridge's product-mix strategy; the specific target of 50% returning revenue is that brand's goal, not a universal benchmark.
Category expansion requires product-development capability many small stores lack.

cards.title: Organizational Metric Ladder: Channel ROAS to Holistic MER
cards.summary: Different roles should own different efficiency metrics — ad-level ROAS, channel MER, digital MER — while the CEO watches holistic business MER against targets.
cards.use_when: Setting metric ownership and targets across a marketing/ecommerce team, or deciding which number to optimize at each level.
steps: Assign ad-level ROAS ownership to the channel buyer; channel MER to the paid-media lead; digital MER to the CMO; and holistic business MER to the CEO.
Have the CEO include total business revenue (wholesale, Amazon, international markets) in the top-line MER rather than only digital channels.

Accept varying marketing-to-revenue ratios by margin structure: Ridge reportedly spends up to ~50% of revenue on marketing in some periods at roughly 2x MER, funded by healthy margins — this is high-margin-specific, not a general target.

Keep headcount lean: Ridge's US payroll is around ~7% of revenue with ~45 full-time US employees, while the source notes some modern brands (a hydration brand and beauty brands) run far leaner at $40M–$100M revenue.
Treat these ratios as the source's examples, not benchmarks; derive your own from margins, TAM and channel economics.
Use best-in-class tools (out-of-the-box Shopify, platform ad systems) to avoid scaling headcount unnecessarily; verify current platform capabilities.
caveats: The 50%-of-revenue marketing figure and low payroll ratios are Ridge/source examples tied to high margins and are not applicable universally.
Very lean staffing may trade off service quality or product development; the source frames it as a modern opportunity, not a mandate.

cards.title: Where to Spend Media Tools: MMM vs Incrementality
cards.summary: MMM surveys all channel spend to suggest reallocation, while incrementality tests hold out spend to measure true lift; both are ~1%-of-budget tool categories.
cards.use_when: Choosing between media-mix modeling and incrementality testing (or both) to guide channel allocation for a store spending across multiple channels.
steps: Use MMM (mixed media modeling) to analyze all spend and model reallocation (e.g., shifting budget to TV or Snapchat); it is an older 'gold standard' approach and the source notes it has somewhat fallen out of favor.
Use incrementality/holdout testing to measure actual lift from a channel by withholding spend in matched geographies; the source calls it an established science and notes Meta offers free tests.
Budget roughly 1% of marketing spend across these tools; if they improve performance ~5%, they pay for themselves.
Apply MMM more for macro reallocation and incrementality for validating individual channels; combine as needed.
Adopt incrementality once spend spans multiple channels rather than only relying on platform-reported metrics.
Verify current vendors and pricing (e.g., Northbeam, Measured, and holdout-test tools) before committing, as offerings change.
caveats: MMM is modeling-based and less favored than holdout testing per the source; results depend on data quality.
Tools cost money and require sufficient spend volume for meaningful signal.

cards.title: Mass-Market Product Selection Checklist
cards.summary: Screen product ideas against a checklist: consumable, strong LTV, low SKU count, large TAM, mass-retail viability and 75%+ gross margins.
cards.use_when: Choosing a product category or SKU to launch for a new store or an expansion line.
steps: 1) Prioritize a consumable/replenishable product so customers return on a predictable cadence and supply chains stay simpler.
2) Require strong LTV alongside acquisition — pair a consumable with repeat or subscription behavior.
3) Keep SKU counts low to simplify inventory, creative and operations (a single-flavor gummy is the source's example).
4) Target a large TAM; the source casts fashion as a poor category partly because no wholesale channel wants it cheaply and top retail accounts are small or financially shaky.
5) Favor categories that can reach mass retail (Target, Walmart, Costco named as the three that matter).
6) Require ~75% gross margin minimum (the source raised this from a prior ~70%).
7) Add a vanity/health/social element that broadens appeal.
Verify current retail accounts and category economics; these are the source's opinions and examples, not guarantees.
caveats: These are the speaker's criteria; the 75% margin figure is his stated current threshold, not an industry standard.
The categories were shaped by his experience; your margins and logistics may differ.

cards.title: Session-Scoped Metric Ownership and Guardrails
cards.summary: Different roles own different efficiency metrics — ad-level ROAS for buyers, channel and digital MER for leaders, holistic MER for the CEO — with lean headcount and margin-aware spend.
cards.use_when: Deciding which efficiency metric sits with which team member and how much of revenue to deploy into marketing for a scaling store.
steps: Map metrics to roles: buyer owns individual-ad ROAS; paid-media VP owns channel MER; CMO owns digital MER; CEO owns total-business MER including wholesale, Amazon and international.

Set a top-line MER target that reflects margins: Ridge runs up to ~50% of revenue in marketing sometimes at ~2x MER because margins support it — this is a high-margin example, not a goal for every store.
Keep payroll lean: the source cites ~7% of revenue in payroll at Ridge and other brands doing $40M–$100M with a handful of employees; derive your own sustainable ratio.
Use platform-native and out-of-the-box tools (Shopify, ad platforms) to avoid scaling headcount; verify current capabilities before building custom.
Reassess the mix periodically because channel efficiency and creative performance change.
caveats: Percentages here are specific examples from one nine-figure business and are not benchmarks.
Aggressive marketing spend depends on margins; lower-margin stores cannot copy it.
